title: Indian Students Abroad Face Deadly Crisis: 26 Killed in Violent Attacks, Deportations Surge
excerpt: Parliamentary data reveals 26 Indian students killed in violent incidents in Canada and the US between 2018 and 2025, while deportations from America surged to 3,567 in 2025 and visa rejections hit record highs.
body:
• Between 2018 and 2025, 26 Indian students were killed in violent attacks in Canada (17) and the United States (9), according to India's Parliament data from February 2026.
  • The US deported 3,567 Indian citizens in 2025, with another 1,076 removed by June 2026 under the Trump administration's enforcement drive.
  • Canada rejected 74% of Indian student visa applications in August 2025, up from 32% two years earlier.
  • New US regulations capping F-1 visa stays at four years, effective September 2026, could upend plans for roughly 330,000 Indian students in American institutions.

A mounting toll of violent deaths, surging deportations, and an increasingly hostile visa environment have converged into a full-blown crisis for Indian students overseas. The data, drawn from parliamentary records and immigration authorities across multiple countries, paints a picture of systemic vulnerability that extends far beyond isolated tragedies.

The Death Toll

In February 2026, India's Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh told Parliament that 17 Indian students had been killed in violent attacks in Canada between 2018 and 2025 — the highest for any single country. The United States accounted for nine, followed by Australia with three, and one each in the UK, China, Denmark, Germany, Grenada, and Kyrgyzstan, according to data provided in response to a question from AIMIM MP Asaduddin Owaisi.

Violent deaths represent only a fraction of the broader toll. MEA data indicates at least 842 Indian students died abroad between 2018 and 2024 from all causes — roughly one death every three days. Canada recorded 172 total student deaths over five years, the US 108, the UK 58, and Australia 57.

Recent incidents have kept the issue in the spotlight. In May 2026, Vidhi Meghani, a 22-year-old law student from Gujarat, was stabbed to death in Canada's Niagara region. In December 2025, Shivank Avasthi, a 20-year-old life sciences student at the University of Toronto Scarborough, was gunned down near campus. Days later, Himanshi Khurana, 30, was killed in Toronto in what police described as intimate partner violence.

"The sudden surge of deaths among Indian students is alarming and suspicious."

— Dr. Lakshmi Thalanki, researcher, Boston

Deportations Spike Under Trump

The United States deported 3,567 Indian citizens in 2025, with another 1,076 removed by June 2026, according to the MEA. Approximately 18,000 undocumented Indians now face removal as the Trump administration prepares a broader deportation drive, a Dainik Bhaskar investigation found.

On February 5, 2025, 104 Indians were flown to Amritsar aboard a US military aircraft, some reportedly bound in handcuffs and ankle shackles. The images sparked outrage across India and sharp criticism in Parliament. Immigration attorneys report that detained individuals are now being sent directly to detention centres with limited access to legal representation.

Visa Doors Closing

Canada rejected 74% of Indian student visa applications in August 2025, according to IRCC data provided to Reuters — more than double the 32% rejection rate in August 2023. The global rejection rate held at around 40%, while Chinese applicants faced just 24%. Indian applicant volume itself collapsed from 19,175 to 3,920 over the same period as Ottawa slashed study permits and flagged fraud concerns.

In the United States, the Department of Homeland Security published a rule on July 16 eliminating the decades-old "duration of status" framework for F-1 visa holders. Effective September 15, 2026, international students face a strict four-year cap, with extensions requiring direct federal approval. The post-graduation grace period drops from 60 to 30 days.

The rule could impact some 330,000 Indian students currently enrolled — the largest international cohort in the country. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India is in contact with Washington to "minimise the difficulties that our people face."

Diaspora Impact

For the Indian diaspora, the crisis touches multiple pressure points. Families who have invested lakhs in overseas education now watch their children navigate physical danger, legal vulnerability, and bureaucratic hostility. When deaths occur, families confront agonising repatriation processes and foreign legal systems they cannot navigate, with consular support that researchers describe as reactive rather than preventive.

With approximately 1.33 million Indian students studying abroad and the two most popular destinations tightening every lever, the crisis shows no signs of easing.
